monte-alban.summary: A city levelled from a mountaintop, and the source of some of the earliest writing in the Americas.

nazca-lines.summary: Hundreds of figures and straight lines scraped into the desert over a thousand years, most plausibly walked as ritual paths, and legible in full only from the surrounding hills or the air.

ramayana.summary: The Sanskrit epic of Rama, Sita and Ravana, ascribed to Valmiki. With the Mahabharata it is one of the two great epics of the subcontinent and the source of retellings across South and Southeast Asia.
ramayana.significance: Its reach is the point. Versions belong to Thailand, Indonesia, Cambodia and Laos, which makes it one of the few narratives to have become foundational to cultures that never shared a state.
ramayana.note: The core books are generally dated to roughly the 5th–4th centuries BCE, with books 1 and 7 added later; the text reached something like its present form by about the 3rd century CE. Traditional accounts place the events far earlier, in the Treta Yuga.

valmiki.summary: The poet to whom the Ramayana is ascribed, and with it the sloka metre that Sanskrit narrative verse used for the next two thousand years.
valmiki.note: Tradition calls him the adi-kavi, the first poet, and the bracket is the period of the Ramayana's composition rather than a recorded life. The text grew over centuries, so a single author is a simplification the tradition itself makes.

phidias-greek-sculpture.summary: In two generations Greek sculptors went from rigid frontal figures to bodies with weight shifted onto one leg — a way of carving the human body that European art returned to twice, at the Renaissance and again in the eighteenth century.
phidias-greek-sculpture.note: Almost nothing survives in the original. The Parthenon figures are Phidias's by attribution and workshop, and most famous Greek statues are known only through Roman marble copies of lost bronzes.

analects.summary: The record of Confucius's sayings, put together after his death and the basis of the Chinese examination system for centuries.
analects.note: Assembled by later disciples over generations; the layers are still debated.

socrates.summary: Wrote nothing, but by relentless questioning turned philosophy from speculation about nature to examination of how one ought to live. Executed by Athens for impiety and corrupting the young.
socrates.significance: He wrote nothing, and is known only through students. The shortest gap in the record file, and still enough for two portraits that do not fully agree.

hippocrates.summary: Separated medicine from superstition by insisting that disease has natural causes and should be studied through careful observation.

image.credit: Paulus Pontius / After Peter Paul Rubens

plague-of-athens.summary: Struck Athens during the Peloponnesian War, killing perhaps a quarter of the population including Pericles, and is often counted among the reasons Athens lost.
plague-of-athens.note: The pathogen is still unidentified; typhoid fever and typhus are the most argued-for candidates.

plato.summary: Argued that the changing world we see is a shadow of unchanging forms, and founded the Academy, which lasted three centuries.
plato.significance: The Academy lasted three centuries. Western philosophy has been described, not entirely as a joke, as a series of footnotes to him.

daodejing.summary: The foundational Daoist text, traditionally ascribed to Laozi but probably composite.

mahabharata.summary: The longest epic poem known, recounting the Kurukshetra war between the Pandavas and Kauravas and absorbing an enormous body of philosophical and legal material.
mahabharata.significance: Roughly ten times the length of the Iliad and Odyssey combined, and it absorbs the Bhagavad Gita as a late insertion - a philosophy that entered the world embedded in a war story.
mahabharata.note: Composed and expanded over roughly eight centuries; the Bhagavad Gita is a later insertion usually dated to the first centuries BCE or CE.

plato-on-socrates.summary: Socrates wrote nothing. Everything attributed to him comes from students writing within a generation of his execution — the shortest gap here, and still enough for two portraits that do not fully agree.
plato-on-socrates.note: Whether the dialogues report Socrates or use him as a mouthpiece for Plato is the "Socratic problem", and is unresolved.

texts.title: Classical texts at the Internet Sacred Text Archive

aristotle.summary: Built the first formal logic and wrote systematically on almost everything, from biology to ethics to poetry, dominating European thought for nearly two millennia.
aristotle.significance: His authority became so total that disputing him was heresy for a millennium - which made overturning him, from Galileo onward, the founding act of modern science.

kautilya.summary: Political theorist and minister to the first Mauryan emperor, whose Arthashastra treats statecraft, economics and espionage without moralising.
kautilya.note: The Arthashastra reached its present form centuries later; how much is his is disputed.

epicurus.summary: Taught that pleasure rightly understood means freedom from pain and fear, best found in friendship and modest living.

zeno-stoic.summary: Founded Stoicism, which holds that virtue is the only real good and that peace comes from separating what we control from what we do not.

euclid.summary: Organised geometry into a system of definitions, postulates and proofs whose structure set the pattern for mathematical argument ever after.
euclid.note: Almost nothing personal is known; the dates bracket his active period in Alexandria.

image.credit: Jusepe de Ribera (Spanish / Italian, 1591 - 1652) (1591 - 1652) – artist (Spanish / Italian) Details on Google Art Project

maurya-empire.summary: Founded by Chandragupta Maurya, the first empire to unify most of the subcontinent, governed from Pataliputra.
maurya-empire.significance: The first state to hold most of the subcontinent at once, and the benchmark every later Indian empire was measured against, including the Mughals two thousand years later.

ashoka.summary: Mauryan emperor who, after the carnage at Kalinga, embraced Buddhism and inscribed edicts of dhamma on rock and pillar across his empire.
ashoka.significance: His edicts are the earliest deciphered Indian writing after the Indus script, and they are a ruler publicly regretting his own war - which is close to unique in the ancient record.

maya-writing.summary: A fully developed logosyllabic script, the only one in the pre-Columbian Americas able to record any spoken sentence, paired with a calendar tracking cycles over millions of days.

thiruvalluvar.display: c. 300 BCE – 100 CE to c. 200 BCE – 200 CE
thiruvalluvar.summary: Author of the Tirukkural, 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love that belong to no one religion — which is why Jains, Hindus and Christians have each claimed him.
thiruvalluvar.note: The dating spans some five centuries and is argued on linguistic grounds. The Tamil Nadu government's official date of 31 BCE is a convention, not a finding.

zero-decimal-system.summary: Treating zero as a number rather than an absence made written arithmetic practical and underlies every calculation since.
zero-decimal-system.significance: Treating nothing as a number is the single most consequential notational change in mathematics. Every calculation you have ever done depends on it.
zero-decimal-system.note: Place value appears in Indian texts over several centuries; Brahmagupta in 628 CE gives the first surviving rules for zero as a number.

archimedes.summary: Worked out the principles of levers and buoyancy and came close to integral calculus while calculating areas and volumes.

eratosthenes.summary: Measured the circumference of the Earth from the difference in shadow lengths between two Egyptian cities, and came remarkably close.

qin-dynasty.summary: Shi Huangdi unified the warring states, standardised script, weights and axle widths, and began the Great Wall and the terracotta army.

xiongnu.summary: The first great steppe confederation, powerful enough to extract tribute from Han China and to make wall-building a matter of state policy.

han-dynasty.summary: Four centuries of Chinese imperial rule that established the Confucian bureaucratic state and opened the Silk Road.
han-dynasty.significance: Contemporary with Rome and comparable in scale, yet the two empires knew each other mostly as rumours at the ends of the Silk Road. The overlap on this timeline is the point.

ajanta-caves.summary: Thirty rock-cut halls in a Deccan ravine holding the largest body of surviving early Indian painting, sealed by the jungle until 1819 and still the reference for what classical Indian art looked like in colour.
ajanta-caves.note: Two phases separated by roughly six centuries — a Satavahana-era group and a much larger Vakataka-era one in the fifth century. The bracket spans both.

paper-making.summary: Cheap writing material, which took roughly a thousand years to reach Europe by way of Samarkand and the Islamic world.
paper-making.significance: Cheap writing material is the precondition for almost everything printed, which is why the printing press arrives in Europe only once paper has.
paper-making.note: Cai Lun is traditionally credited in 105 CE, but fragments predate him by up to three centuries; he probably improved and standardised a process already in use.

silk-road.summary: Overland routes linking China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean, carrying silk, spices, paper, Buddhism and plague alike.

teotihuacan.summary: A city of well over a hundred thousand people laid out on a grid, among the largest in the world at its height. The Aztecs found it long abandoned and named it the place where the gods were born.
teotihuacan.note: Who built and ruled it is unknown. It has no surviving royal portraits or king lists, which is unusual enough to have prompted theories of collective rule.

virgil.summary: Author of the Aeneid, written to give Rome a founding epic to set beside Homer's, and left unfinished at his death with orders to burn it that Augustus overruled.

korea-three-kingdoms.summary: Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla contended for the peninsula for seven centuries, transmitting Buddhism and Chinese writing on to Japan along the way.

ovid.summary: Whose Metamorphoses carried Greek and Roman myth into European art wholesale, and who was exiled to the Black Sea by Augustus for a reason he never stated plainly.

pali-canon-written.summary: Roughly four centuries after the Buddha's death, his teachings were written on palm leaves in Sri Lanka because war and famine threatened the monks who held them in memory.
pali-canon-written.significance: Four centuries between the teacher and the text. Theravada tradition holds the oral transmission exact, so the gap is one of writing, not necessarily of content.
pali-canon-written.note: Sri Lankan chronicles place the writing at Aluvihare during a famine, around 29 BCE. Theravada tradition holds the oral transmission to have been exact, so the gap is a gap in writing, not necessarily in content.

texts.title: Buddhist texts at the Internet Sacred Text Archive

roman-empire.summary: From Augustus to the deposition of Romulus Augustulus, an empire encircling the Mediterranean whose law, language and roads outlasted it.
roman-empire.significance: Its collapse in the west is the reference point Europe measured itself against for a thousand years, and the reason 'the fall of Rome' still functions as shorthand for civilisational loss.

jesus.summary: An itinerant Jewish teacher in Roman Judaea whose execution and the movement that followed became Christianity.
jesus.note: Birth is placed a few years before 1 CE because the calendar's sixth-century calculation was slightly off. The crucifixion is usually dated to 30 or 33 CE.
